references.text: The temple was rebuilt during the reign of Darius. The book of Ezra describes the completion of the second temple ([ref:Esra 6:15|Ezra 6:15]), which Herod later expanded and beautified—a construction project that had been ongoing for 46 years when the Jews referred to it in their conversation with Jesus.

Jesus had just said, 'Destroy this temple, and I will raise it up in three days' ([ref:Joh 2:19|John 2:19]). The Jews' response in verse 20 shows that they misunderstood him literally, while he was speaking about his body.
The next verse explains that the temple Jesus spoke of was his own body ([ref:Joh 2:21|John 2:21]), something the disciples only understood after the resurrection.

During Jesus' trial, his words about destroying the temple and rebuilding it in three days were used as an accusation against him ([ref:Matt 26:61|Matthew 26:61]). The Jews' reaction shows that the statement was remembered and distorted.
Those who passed by the cross mocked Jesus with the words about destroying the temple and rebuilding it in three days ([ref:Matt 27:40|Matthew 27:40]), a direct reference to that same conversation.
Also in Mark's account of the trial, Jesus is accused of saying he would destroy the temple and build a new one in three days ([ref:Mark 14:58|Mark 14:58]).
At the cross, passersby mock Jesus with reference to his words about the temple ([ref:Mark 15:29|Mark 15:29]).

Stephen was accused of saying that Jesus from Nazareth would destroy the temple ([ref:Apg 6:14|Acts 6:14]). The accusation is based on the same misunderstanding of Jesus' words that the Jews expressed in John 2:20.

Solomon's construction of the first temple took seven years ([ref:1 Kong 6:1-38|1 Kings 6:1–38]). Although the Jews in John 2:20 refer to Herod's expansion of the second temple, the building history of the first temple provides background on the significance of the temple in Israel.
